children.text: The Front Door of the Revenue Cycle

The revenue cycle begins before any care is delivered, at scheduling and registration. This is the front door, and what happens here quietly determines the fate of the eventual claim. Two activities dominate: pre-registration, which captures the patient's demographic and insurance information, and insurance verification, which confirms that coverage actually exists for the planned service.

Pre-registration ideally happens before the visit — often while the patient is still on the phone scheduling — so that any problem (an inactive plan, a wrong ID, a missing authorization) can be caught and fixed while there is still time. Registration then confirms and completes that information when the patient arrives.

These steps feel like clerical busywork, but they are among the highest-leverage activities in the entire cycle. A clean front door means clean claims downstream; a sloppy one guarantees denials weeks later, when they are far more expensive to fix.

Pre-registration captures patient demographic and insurance information before the visit; insurance verification confirms active coverage for the planned service. Together they are the front door that determines whether the eventual claim can be paid.
Why the Front-End Matters So Much

The data is blunt: front-end issues cause roughly half of all claim denials, and registration plus eligibility problems alone account for a little over one-quarter of denied claims. The very first step of the cycle is also its single largest source of preventable revenue loss.

Most of these denials are entirely preventable. Over 20 percent of denied claims involve human input errors — a mistyped member ID, a misspelled name, a wrong date of birth. Eligibility systems match patient data against the payer's enrollment records exactly, so even a small mismatch causes an automatic rejection. The care was fine; the data entry was not.

This is why the front-end deserves disproportionate attention. A denial prevented at registration costs almost nothing; the same denial caught after submission must be researched, corrected, resubmitted, and followed up — at a cost of $25 to $181 per claim and weeks of delay. The economics overwhelmingly favor getting it right at the front door.

children.text: How Verification Works: The 270/271 Transaction

Insurance verification is largely automated through a standardized electronic exchange. The provider sends the payer an electronic eligibility inquiry — a HIPAA "270" transaction — and the payer returns an electronic response, the "271" transaction. This 270/271 pair is the technical backbone of eligibility verification.

Done in real time, the round trip typically returns a response within about 10 to 30 seconds — fast enough to verify a patient during check-in. The 271 response is rich: it can confirm whether coverage is active and its effective dates, list benefit details by service type, report copay, coinsurance, deductible, and out-of-pocket maximum status, flag whether prior authorization is required, and confirm network participation.

That last set of details is what makes verification so valuable — it not only confirms the patient is covered but surfaces exactly what they will owe and whether extra steps (like prior authorization) are needed before the service. This is the same standardized-data, EDI machinery that runs throughout RCM, applied to the very first step.

children.text: Coordination of Benefits

A particular verification challenge is coordination of benefits (COB): determining the correct order of payment when a patient has more than one insurance plan. If a patient has both a primary and a secondary payer, claims must go to the primary first, and only the remaining balance to the secondary.

Getting COB wrong is a common denial cause: a claim sent to the secondary payer first, or to a plan that is actually secondary, will be rejected with instructions to bill the correct primary. The eligibility exchange helps here, since the 270/271 supports coordination-of-benefits information, but it still requires the front-end staff to ask the right questions and record which plan is primary.

COB is a good example of why verification is more than a yes/no coverage check. It is about establishing the complete, correct picture of who pays, in what order, and for what — so the claim goes to the right payer the first time. A patient with Medicare and a commercial plan, or two employed spouses each with coverage, needs this sorted before the claim ever goes out.

body.content:
A patient is covered by their own employer plan and, as a dependent, by their spouse's plan. If the front-end staff bill the spouse's plan as primary when the patient's own plan should be primary, the claim is denied and must be rebilled in the correct order.
The care was appropriate and covered — the loss came entirely from getting the payment order wrong at verification, a classic preventable front-end denial.

children.text: Building a Strong Front-End Process

Because the stakes are so high and the errors so preventable, organizations invest heavily in front-end discipline. The core practices are straightforward: verify eligibility before every visit (not just at the first), confirm and re-confirm demographic data against a photo ID, and run real-time 270/271 checks so problems surface while they can still be fixed.

Automation is increasingly central. Real-time and batch eligibility tools can verify entire schedules of upcoming patients automatically, flagging inactive coverage, term dates, and authorization requirements before anyone arrives. This shifts the front-end from reactive (fix the denial later) to proactive (prevent it now), which is exactly where the economics point.

The mindset to instill is that the front-end is where money is saved, not spent. Every minute invested verifying coverage and cleaning up patient data at intake prevents a multiplied cost downstream. The next lessons — prior authorization and financial counseling — build directly on this foundation, completing the front-end's job of setting up a claim that can actually be paid.

body.message: Coverage changes — patients switch jobs, plans terminate, benefits reset annually. Verifying eligibility only at the first encounter and assuming it holds is a frequent cause of denials. Re-verify before each visit, ideally with an automated real-time check against the schedule.
body.title: Verify Every Visit, Not Just the First
